findings.title: CORS Wildcard with Credentials
findings.impact:
Any origin can make credentialed cross-site requests to this API.
Combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, this enables
cross-site request forgery and session theft from any website.
findings.remediation:
Replace the wildcard with an explicit allowlist of trusted origins.
Never combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with Allow-Credentials: true.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
response.headers["Access-Control-Allow-Origin"] = "*"
response.headers["Access-Control-Allow-Credentials"] = "true"

# After (fixed):
ALLOWED_ORIGINS = {"https://app.example.com"}
origin = request.headers.get("Origin", "")
if origin in ALLOWED_ORIGINS:
    response.headers["Access-Control-Allow-Origin"] = origin
    response.headers["Vary"] = "Origin"

findings.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
findings.evidence: GET /user/<int:user_id> — no ownership check found in handler body
findings.impact: An attacker can access or modify records belonging to any other user by changing the ID in the URL.
findings.remediation:
Verify that the authenticated user owns the requested resource before returning it.
Compare session user ID to the requested resource's owner ID.

findings.title: Route with No Authentication
findings.evidence: GET /admin — handler: admin_panel — auth decorators: none
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and its data.
findings.remediation: Add an authentication decorator (e.g. @login_required, @jwt_required) before the route handler.

findings.title: Flask/FastAPI Debug Mode Enabled
findings.impact:
Flask debug mode exposes an interactive Werkzeug debugger console in the browser.
An attacker who triggers any exception gets a Python REPL with full server access.
findings.remediation: Set debug=False in production, or read from an environment variable.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
app.run(debug=True)

# After (fixed):
import os
app.run(debug=os.getenv('FLASK_DEBUG', 'false').lower() == 'true')

findings.title: Unpinned Dependencies
findings.impact:
Unpinned dependencies are resolved at install time to whatever the latest version is.
A supply-chain attack or accidentally breaking change in a dependency can be silently
introduced into the production build.
findings.remediation: Pin every dependency to an exact version (==) or a narrow range (>=x,<x+1).
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
flask
requests

# After (fixed):
flask==3.0.3
requests==2.32.3

findings.title: Hardcoded Secret or API Key
findings.impact:
Hardcoded secrets committed to source control are trivially discoverable by anyone
with repository access, or via git history even after deletion.
findings.remediation: Move secrets to environment variables or a secret manager. Add .env to .gitignore.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
SECRET_KEY = "my-super-secret-key-1234"

# After (fixed):
import os
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["SECRET_KEY"]

findings.title: MD5 or SHA1 Used for Password Hashing
findings.impact:
MD5 and SHA1 are fast hash functions not designed for password storage.
An attacker with the hash database can crack most passwords in minutes
using a GPU and rainbow tables.
findings.remediation: Use bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2-SHA256 with a per-user salt and high iteration count.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
hashed = hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest()

# After (fixed — using PBKDF2):
import hashlib, os
salt = os.urandom(16)
hashed = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', password.encode(), salt, 260000)

findings.title: JWT with 'none' Algorithm or Absent Verification
findings.impact:
The 'none' algorithm disables JWT signature verification entirely.
Any attacker can forge a token with arbitrary claims (e.g. admin role)
without knowing the secret key.
findings.remediation: Always specify a strong algorithm (HS256, RS256) and verify the signature.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
token = jwt.encode(payload, "", algorithm="none")
data = jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})

# After (fixed):
import os
SECRET = os.environ["JWT_SECRET"]
token = jwt.encode(payload, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")
data = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])

findings.title: Dangerous Code Execution (eval/exec/os.system)
findings.impact:
Allows arbitrary code or OS command execution if user-controlled data reaches this call.
An attacker can read files, exfiltrate data, install malware, or take over the server.
findings.remediation:
- Replace eval() with ast.literal_eval() for safe literal parsing.
- Replace os.system() with subprocess.run(shell=False, args=[...]).
- Never pass user input to exec() or shell=True.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
result = eval(request.args.get('expr'))
os.system(f"convert {user_input}.jpg output.png")

# After (fixed):
import ast
result = ast.literal_eval(request.args.get('expr'))  # literals only

import subprocess
subprocess.run(["convert", safe_filename, "output.png"], shell=False)

findings.title: Missing Input Validation on Request Fields
findings.evidence: Inputs used: ['name'] — no validation found in handler
findings.impact: Request fields are used without type checking, length limits, or format validation, enabling injection or logic bypass.
findings.remediation:
Validate and sanitise every input from request.args, request.form, and request.get_json()
before using it in queries, file operations, or business logic.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
user_id = request.args.get("id")
db.query(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}")

# After (fixed):
try:
    user_id = int(request.args.get("id", ""))
except ValueError:
    return jsonify({"error": "id must be an integer"}), 400
db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (user_id,))

findings.title: SQL Injection via String Formatting
findings.evidence: query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
findings.impact: Full database read, modification, and potential deletion via SQL injection.
findings.remediation: Use parameterised queries. Never interpolate user input directly into SQL strings.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
cursor.execute(query)

# After (fixed):
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))
# or with SQLAlchemy:
db.execute(text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = :name"), {"name": name})

findings.title: No Logging on Failed Authentication
findings.evidence: POST /login — no logging call found in login handler
findings.impact:
Failed login attempts are not recorded, making it impossible to detect
brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, or account enumeration.
findings.remediation:
Log every failed authentication attempt with timestamp, username, and source IP.
Consider rate limiting after N failures.

findings.title: Stack Trace Returned to Client
findings.impact:
Full stack traces reveal internal file paths, library versions, function names,
and variable values — a roadmap that makes other attacks much easier to develop.
findings.remediation: Catch exceptions at the top level, log the trace server-side, and return only a generic error message to the client.
findings.fixed_code:
# Before (vulnerable):
except Exception as e:
    import traceback
    return jsonify({"error": str(e), "traceback": traceback.format_exc()}), 500

# After (fixed):
except Exception:
    logger.exception("Unhandled error in endpoint")
    return jsonify({"error": "An internal error occurred"}), 500

chains.name: Full Database Takeover
chains.description: An unauthenticated sensitive route combined with SQL injection enables full database read, modification, and deletion without any credentials.
chains.narrative: Step 1: The /admin or other sensitive route is accessible without authentication (A01-NOAUTH-001). Step 2: A SQL injection vulnerability on a search or data endpoint (A05-SQL-001) allows arbitrary database queries. Together: an attacker accesses the admin endpoint to enumerate structure, then uses SQL injection to exfiltrate, modify, or delete all database records.

chains.name: Remote Code Execution via Open Admin
chains.description: An unauthenticated admin route plus an eval/exec call allows arbitrary OS command execution by any unauthenticated user.
chains.narrative: Step 1: Admin or management endpoints are accessible without authentication (A01-NOAUTH-001). Step 2: eval() or exec() is called with user-controlled input (A05-EXEC-001). Together: an attacker sends crafted input to the open admin endpoint, achieving arbitrary code execution on the server with the app's OS privileges.

chains.name: Authentication Bypass via JWT Forgery
chains.description: A JWT with algorithm='none' combined with a protected route means any attacker can forge an admin token and access protected resources.
chains.narrative: Step 1: The JWT implementation accepts algorithm='none', disabling signature verification (A04-JWT-001). Step 2: Admin routes lack authentication (A01-NOAUTH-001). Together: an attacker crafts a JWT claiming admin role without knowing any secret, then accesses all admin functionality.

chains.name: Credential Harvest via Debug Console
chains.description: Flask debug=True exposes an interactive Python console; combined with hardcoded secrets, all credentials are immediately available.
chains.narrative: Step 1: Flask is running with debug=True, exposing the Werkzeug interactive debugger on any exception page (A02-DEBUG-001). Step 2: Hardcoded secrets exist in the source (A04-SECRET-001). Together: an attacker triggers an exception to access the debugger console, reads the running source, and extracts all hardcoded credentials.

chains.name: IDOR + Weak Hash = Account Takeover
chains.description: Insecure Direct Object Reference combined with MD5/SHA1 password hashing enables account takeover: enumerate user IDs via IDOR, then crack the weak hashes.
chains.narrative: Step 1: User data endpoints return records for any ID without ownership checks (A01-IDOR-001), allowing enumeration of user records. Step 2: Passwords are hashed with MD5 (A04-WEAKHASH-001), which can be cracked in seconds with GPU rainbow tables. Together: an attacker enumerates user records, extracts password hashes, cracks them, and logs in as any user.
